title: Recording a macro
summary: Developer › Record Macro writes VBA while you work: every click, including the mistakes. Absolute references record exact cells; Use Relative References records moves from the active cell. Run the result from the Macros list, a shortcut key or a button.
objectives: Record a macro with a good name, a description and a shortcut key.
Choose absolute or relative references before you record.
Run a macro from Alt+F8, a Ctrl+Shift shortcut and a button on the sheet.
Plan a recording so it holds only the steps you want.

slides.h: Name it, then do the steps
p: Developer, Record Macro. Give it a name, optionally a shortcut and a description, and choose where to store it. Click OK and every click you make is written down as VBA, until you click Stop Recording.
**Name:** starts with a letter, no spaces, and can’t look like a cell address: Q1 or TAX2026 won’t do.
**Store macro in:** This Workbook (usually), New Workbook, or Personal Macro Workbook (Lesson 1.4).
**Description:** say what it does; it’s written into the code as a comment.
In real life: names macros with a verb and a noun: FormatHeader, MarkDispatched, SaveAsPDF. Meena can guess what each one does.

p: The recorder doesn’t know what you meant. It writes every selection, every scroll to another cell, and every mistake you correct. So plan the steps, practise once, then record.
Click where you need to start **before** you press Record.
Mistakes you fix are recorded twice: once wrong, once right.
Click **Stop Recording** (Developer, or ■ on the status bar) the moment you’re done.
In real life: recorded a macro, sneezed, clicked three random cells, and all three Selects were in the code.

visual.text:
Sub FormatHeader()
'
' FormatHeader Macro
' Bold, light blue header for the orders
'
' Keyboard Shortcut: Ctrl+Shift+H
'
    Range("A1:H1").Select
    Selection.Font.Bold = True
    With Selection.Interior
        .Pattern = xlSolid
        .PatternColorIndex = xlAutomatic
        .Color = 16247773
        .TintAndShade = 0
        .PatternTintAndShade = 0
    End With
    Range("A2").Select
End Sub
notes: You selected A1:H1: the recorder writes a Select
Seven lines for one fill colour: the recorder writes everything the dialog holds
You clicked A2 before stopping: that’s recorded too

p: A shortcut like Ctrl+H would replace Excel’s own Find and Replace while the workbook is open. Hold Shift when you type the letter in the box, and the macro gets Ctrl+Shift+H, which Excel doesn’t use.
The shortcut is written into the code as a comment, so you can see it.
Change it later: Developer › Macros › pick it › **Options…**
Shortcuts work only while the workbook with the macro is open.
In real life: gave a macro Ctrl+S once. Every Save in that workbook ran his macro instead.

check.q: Which of these is a valid macro name?
check.explain: No spaces, starts with a letter, and doesn’t look like a cell address (AB12 is a cell).

slides.h: Absolute: the same cells every time
p: By default the recorder writes exact addresses. Record a click on I2 and typing Checked, and the macro always writes in I2, whichever cell you’re on when you run it.
Right for fixed places: a header row, a title cell, a sheet layout that never moves.
Wrong for “the cell I’m on now”.
In real life: ran the absolute version on row 6. It wrote Checked in I2 again.

visual.text:
Sub StampChecked()
'
' StampChecked Macro
'
    Range("I2").Select
    ActiveCell.FormulaR1C1 = "Checked"
    Range("I3").Select
End Sub
visual.caption: Recorded with absolute references

slides.h: Relative: moves from where you are
p: Turn on Use Relative References before you record, and the recorder writes moves instead: ActiveCell.Offset(1, 0) means one row down from wherever you are. Now the macro works on any row.
Turn it on **before** you click Record; you can switch it on and off while recording.
**Offset(rows, columns):** positive goes down and right, negative up and left.
The odd .Range("A1") after Offset just means “that one cell”.
In real life: now ticks each order as she checks it: one keystroke per row.

visual.text:
Sub StampChecked()
'
' StampChecked Macro
'
    ActiveCell.FormulaR1C1 = "Checked"
    ActiveCell.Offset(1, 0).Range("A1").Select
End Sub
notes: Types in whichever cell is active
Offset(1, 0): one row down, no columns across
visual.caption: Recorded with Use Relative References on

slides.h: Four ways to run a macro
p: Alt+F8 lists every macro. A Ctrl+Shift shortcut runs one instantly. A button on the sheet is friendliest for other people: Developer, Insert, Button, draw it, and pick the macro. Or add it to the Quick Access Toolbar.
Right-click a button to change its text or assign another macro.
Put buttons above the data, where they won’t cover it.
Name the button for what it does: Format orders, not Button 1.
In real life: never opens the Macros list. She clicks the green button that says Mark checked.

lab.intro: Meena checks each order on the **Orders** sheet and wants two macros: one to format the header, and one to mark the order she’s on as checked. Record them with **Developer › Record Macro**, then make them easy to run.

tasks.prompt: Record a macro called **FormatHeader** that makes **A1:H1** bold with the **light blue** fill (the second colour in the fill menu). Stop recording when you’re done.
hints: Developer › Record Macro, type FormatHeader, OK.
Select A1:H1, then B (bold) and the fill button › the light blue square.
Click Stop Recording (or ■ at the bottom).

points: **Record Macro** writes VBA while you work, until **Stop Recording**; every click is recorded, so plan first.
Names start with a letter, have no spaces, and don’t look like cell addresses.
Absolute references record exact cells; **Use Relative References** records moves with `ActiveCell.Offset(rows, columns)`.
Run macros with **Alt+F8**, a **Ctrl+Shift** shortcut, or a **button** (Developer › Insert).
recap.cheat: Plan, record, stop; relative for “from here”; Ctrl+Shift shortcuts; buttons for other people.
